body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Nurse-led titration of heart failure medicines versus usual cardiology follow-up: a randomised comparison in two hospital clinics","authors":"Achterberg-Moyo L, Castellane-Idris P, Rhee-Okafor D","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Heart Failure Nursing","doi":"10.5555/jhfn.2019.0231","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Background: many patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction remain on starting doses of guideline medicines. Methods: in two hospital clinics we randomly allocated 262 patients to titration by heart failure nurses with fortnightly visits and a written protocol, or to usual cardiology follow-up every three to four months. Results: at 6 months, 58 percent of patients in nurse-led titration and 31 percent in usual follow-up were on at least half the target dose of both a beta blocker and a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor. Hospitalisation for heart failure within 12 months occurred in 9 percent and 16 percent (hazard ratio 0.54, 95 percent CI 0.30 to 0.97). Potassium above 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 3 percent of patients in each group. Conclusions: nurse-led titration reached higher doses sooner without more hyperkalaemia."},{"title":"Nurse-led titration clinics for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Vasquez-Holm R, Oduya-Pritchard K, Lindqvist-Amadi S, Tanaka-Browne E","year":2022,"venue":"Cardiovascular Nursing Reviews","doi":"10.5555/cvnr.2022.0107","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We searched four bibliographic databases to March 2021 for studies comparing titration led by nurses with physician-led titration in adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In total, 11 studies with 2,480 patients met the criteria, seven of them randomised. Nurse-led titration increased the proportion of patients reaching target doses (risk ratio 1.62, 95 percent CI 1.31 to 2.00) and reduced all-cause hospitalisation (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.66 to 0.93). The effect on mortality was imprecise (risk ratio 0.88, 95 percent CI 0.70 to 1.10). Protocols differed in visit frequency and in the medicines titrated, and no included study titrated SGLT2 inhibitors. Risk of bias was moderate in most randomised studies because outcome assessment was not blinded."},{"title":"Titrating four medicine classes in a nurse-led heart failure clinic after SGLT2 inhibitors became available: a service evaluation","authors":"Bramwell-Osei T, Kowalski-Njoroge M","year":2023,"venue":"Heart Failure Service Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We describe the first 176 patients treated in a nurse-led titration clinic that titrates a beta blocker, a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor or ARNI, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Visits were fortnightly, alternating clinic and telephone, with blood tests before each dose change. The median time to the best tolerated regimen was 14 weeks. At 6 months, 71 percent of patients were taking all four classes and 52 percent were on at least half the target dose of each. Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L led to a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist being held in 11 percent of patients, and eGFR fell by more than 30 percent in 4 percent. There was no comparison group, and patients who declined referral were not followed."},{"title":"Patients' experience of telephone and clinic visits for heart failure medicine titration: an interview study","authors":"Moreau-Kinsella A, Obi-Lindgren H","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Cardiovascular Care Experience","doi":"10.5555/jcce.2020.0412","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 22 patients who had completed medicine titration in a nurse-led heart failure clinic. Patients valued seeing or speaking to the same nurse and understanding why each dose changed. Frequent blood tests were the main burden, especially for those who relied on others for transport. Several patients aged over 80 preferred clinic visits to telephone calls because they found it hard to describe dizziness over the phone. Patients who had been admitted during titration often linked the admission to a dose change, whether or not the change was the cause. The findings suggest offering a choice of visit type and explaining in advance how many blood tests titration will need."},{"title":"Safety of rapid up-titration of heart failure medicines in the 90 days after discharge from a district general hospital","authors":"Farouk-Dunmore S, Ahlberg-Chukwu O, Pereira-Nash J","year":2024,"venue":"District Cardiology Practice","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We reviewed 140 consecutive patients discharged after a heart failure admission who started nurse-supported up-titration within two weeks. Over 90 days, symptomatic hypotension that led to a dose reduction occurred in 7 percent, potassium above 6.0 mmol/L in 2 percent and a fall in eGFR of more than 30 percent in 5 percent. No death was judged related to titration by two reviewing cardiologists. Readmission for any cause within 90 days occurred in 18 percent. Patients aged 80 or over had more dose reductions for hypotension. The study had no comparison group and relied on hospital results, so tests done in primary care may have been missed."},{"title":"Competences for non-medical prescribers who titrate heart failure medicines: a consensus framework","authors":"Heart Failure Nurse Prescribing Working Group","year":2017,"venue":"Northgate Heart Failure Practice Notes","doi":"10.5555/nhfpn.2017.0033","providerType":"practice guideline","abstract":"A working group of heart failure nurses, pharmacists and cardiologists agreed by a two-round consensus process the competences a non-medical prescriber needs before titrating heart failure medicines without a doctor's review of each change. The framework lists 18 competences in four domains: assessment of congestion and blood pressure, interpretation of potassium and kidney function results, dose adjustment rules for each medicine class, and referral thresholds. It recommends a written titration protocol signed off by a named cardiologist, supervised practice for the first 20 patients, and a review of safety events every six months. The framework does not report outcomes and predates the routine use of SGLT2 inhibitors."},{"title":"Deprivation, travel distance and missed titration visits in a heart failure nurse service","authors":"Ncube-Harrington P, Solberg-Adeyemi F","year":2025,"venue":"Health Equity in Cardiology","doi":"10.5555/heic.2025.0016","providerType":"cohort study","abstract":"We examined 612 patients referred to a heart failure nurse titration service over three years. Missed titration visits were more common in the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods (24 percent of scheduled visits) than in the least deprived fifth (9 percent). Patients living more than 20 miles from the clinic missed more visits and took longer to reach their best tolerated regimen. After the service added telephone visits with blood tests at community sites, the gap in missed visits between the most and least deprived fifths narrowed from 15 to 6 percentage points. Patients who needed an interpreter were under-represented among referrals compared with the local heart failure population."}]}
